## Detection model

We index year with $k$, site with $j$, and observations (individual surveys) with $i$.

For nocturnal surveys, we record the time to detection at each survey. For sites with a detection, let time to detection be $^dt_{i}$.

We let $^dt_{i} \sim \text{Exp}(\lambda)$.

Let survey time be $^vt_{i}$.

For a given survey effort (in time) then, the conditional probability of detection, i.e. $P(\text{detect} | \text{present} \cap \text{nocturnal survey}) = 1-e^{-\lambda ^vt_{i}}$.

We also have another method for detecting toads, which are informal interviews of landholders. For these, we simply set $P(\text{detect} | \text{present} \cap \text{interview}) = p$

## Occupancy model

So now we need a model for whether toads are present, or not in a given year.

We assume a straight line invasion front defined by $y_k = ax+b_k$. That is, a straight line with an intercept that varies between years. The perpendicular distance between site, $j$, and our line is given by:

$$d_{jk} = \frac{(y_j-ax_j-b_k)}{\sqrt{1+a^2}}$$

We then define a simple step function that determines occupancy relative to the line.

$$H(d_{jk}) = 
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } d_{jk} \geq 0 \\ 
0 & \text{if } d_{jk} < 0 
\end{cases}$$

This gives us our final probability of detection:

$p_{ijk} = H(d_{jk})\times p_i$ where,

$$p_i =
\begin{cases}
p & \text{if } \text{interview} \\
e^{-\lambda^vt_i} & \text{if } \text{survey}
\end{cases}
$$

We then specify our likelihood of observing toads as:

$$o_{ijk} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p_{ijk})$$
